transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Nice to meet you. I, uh, I guess I'm here because... well, it's just been a series of things lately. What really brings me in is that I keep messing up these little things. It sounds silly when you say it out loud, but it's happening all the time now. Like, just the other day down at the senior center, I was signing up for this woodworking class. I was so sure I wrote down 2:00 PM on the sheet, but I show up and it turns out I wrote down 10:00 AM. And I completely missed it. It's just... frustrating, you know? And it's not just that. I was working on a birdhouse in the garage—I like to tinker out there since I retired—and I swear to you, I measured this one piece of pine board. I looked right at the tape measure, but I must have skipped over the small lines, the little fractions of an inch, because I went and made the cut, and wouldn't you know it, the thing was a hair short. Completely ruined the piece. I had to start all over. It's just these tiny, careless mistakes, over and over. I read something, but I don't really *read* it, if that makes sense. I just skim right past the important details, the small print, and then I end up looking foolish or having to redo my work. It's like my brain just doesn't want to bother with the fine details anymore, and it's starting to really get under my skin.
Have you noticed these kinds of careless mistakes and trouble with details happening your whole life, or did this really start only recently?

Well, you know, my wife asked me something similar just the other day when I was complaining about that birdhouse. She told me I have always been like this. And I had to, well, I had to really stop and think about it, because you get to be sixty-two and the years just sort of blend together, do they not? But I started thinking back to when I was just a little kid, going to elementary school. I remember my mother used to keep all my old report cards in this big metal fruitcake tin in the hall closet. And every single year, it was the exact same story from the teachers. 

I mean, they all wrote these notes saying I was a bright boy, that I had potential, but I was always forgetting my reading books at school, or I would actually sit down at the kitchen table and do the homework and then completely lose the paper before I could even hand it in. It was just a constant battle for my poor mother. And the teachers always wrote that I was just staring out the window, watching the cars go by or looking at the clouds, unless somebody physically walked over and kept me on track. 

So, to answer your question, no, it is definitely not a new thing. It is just... well, when you work for forty years, you have a routine, you know? You have a supervisor keeping you in line and telling you what needs doing. But now that I am retired and making my own schedule, it is like all those old habits from when I was ten years old are coming right back to the surface and driving me absolutely crazy. It is like I am back in third grade all over again, just drifting off and missing the details, and it really makes you wonder how you managed to get by for so long without noticing it as much, but I suppose life was just more structured back then.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes a lifelong pattern (confirmed by childhood report cards and parental report) of inattentive symptoms—careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention to detail, losing items, distractibility, and forgetfulness—persisting from elementary school into adulthood. Symptoms are consistent across settings (school, home, work, retirement activities) and cause functional impairment now that external structure (work supervision) is absent. No reported history of hyperactivity/impulsivity, but the core inattentive criteria are robustly met, supporting ADHD diagnosis (ICD-10 F90.0, used broadly for ADHD in absence of separate inattentive-only code).
